prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form and actions, which made possible a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B010 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The argument is that incretin biology is a complete arc from physiology (the incretin effect, GLP-1 secretion and insulinotropic action) through peptide identification (the active GLP-1(7-36) form) and receptor pharmacology to drugs with large, independently replicated benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism is stable, the randomized evidence is deep across several agents, and recognition is timely if not overdue. Having listened to colleagues, I am moving from my opening trio to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov: this is a prize for the discovery and the mechanism, and the discovery claims are cleaner than the translational one under a three-person cap. Five of six openings converged on the same trio, and I find the attribution reasoning persuasive on its merits.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the three-person limit forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose design of the acylated, long-acting analogues is what turned the hormone into liraglutide and semaglutide, and who is the credited name closest to the drugs that actually changed care. A discovery-only trio risks honouring physiology while omitting the step that created the therapy. There is also an unresolved priority question around Mojsov versus other early GLP-1 work (Habener is not on the credited list), which I cannot verify from the file, and the long-term safety and the central mechanisms of weight loss are still evolving.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked B010 first but treats Knudsen's medicinal chemistry as an industrial development step, and ranked the unfolded protein response (B031) second as a conceptually original, mechanistically complete signalling discovery.
responses.response: I partly accept the framing and have changed my ballot on it: with only three places, I now credit the discoverers over the drug designer, as Sandberg does. I do not accept that industrial origin lowers the weight of Knudsen's contribution, since the Prize has honoured drug-enabling work before, so I record the omission as a real cost rather than a clean judgement. On B031, I agree the science is elegant and the Mori-Walter pairing is clean, but its therapeutic and medical consequence is still emerging, so I would not rank it above a candidate whose human impact is already proven; I keep it behind the clinical candidates.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked optogenetics (B048) second as a general method for causal control of cell types, and notes that credit is contested across six names, proposing Nagel for channelrhodopsin discovery with Deisseroth and Boyden for neuronal deployment.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously, and as a neuroscientist I see how much circuit work in Parkinson's disease, depression and addiction models depends on it. My disagreement is about attribution and medical scope. Bamberg, Nagel, Hegemann, Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenböck all have strong claims, and any three-name selection, including Linnarsson's, leaves out decisive contributors, which makes the prize contestable in a way B010 is not. It is also a research tool whose clinical translation (vision restoration) is early. I therefore keep B048 as a strong but second-tier candidate for this year rather than an alternative I would defend in the final ballot.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked B010 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and placed BCL-2 (B005) third because it showed that cancer can arise from blocked cell death and led directly to venetoclax, while noting the 2002 apoptosis precedent.
responses.response: I agree with Perlmann's B010 trio, which is the configuration I now propose. On B005, I agree the mechanism-to-drug link is unusually clear, but the 2002 prize for the genetics of programmed cell death weakens the novelty claim, and the Tsujimoto and Korsmeyer claims on the translocation make the credit with four names harder than for B010. I would consider B005 only if the committee wanted a cancer-biology part, and I rank it below the targeted-therapy and cell-therapy candidates.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked CAR-T cell therapy (B052) second, as a new therapeutic modality with durable remissions and approved products, while noting that Eshhar and other early CAR designers are missing from the credited list.
responses.response: I agree that B052 is the strongest clinical alternative and that the evidence is now mature, with several approved products and expanding autoimmune use. My qualification, which she also raises, is that the Sadelain, June and Rosenberg trio omits Eshhar and other early designers, and that Rosenberg's contribution is adoptive transfer more than CAR design itself. I would also want to see more late-toxicity and durability data, and solid-tumour efficacy is unresolved. That keeps B052 as my first alternative rather than a competitor to B010 this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle the priority between Mojsov and other early GLP-1 peptide work, including Habener who is not on the credited list, from the supplied evidence alone.
Whether omitting Knudsen is acceptable to colleagues, or whether a two-part configuration (physiology plus drug design) is wanted despite the three-person cap.
Whether the first-round unanimity for B010 reflects a genuine merit judgement or shared anchoring, and how firmly it holds against B052 and B018 once attribution is tested in later rounds.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented ties (a Rockefeller postdoc with Paul Greengard and about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, count unaudited) do not involve any shortlisted candidate, and shared neurology interests alone do not constitute a conflict.
